name: Black vinegar stand-in
blurb: Balsamic is the accepted stand-in for Chinkiang. Cutting it with rice vinegar thins the sweetness back to something Chinese food can use.
method: Stir together and keep in a small bottle by the stove.
Taste against anything you are dressing. If it still reads sweet, push the rice vinegar up to 1:1.
uses: Anywhere a recipe says black vinegar
note: The real bottle is about four dollars and the balsamic sweetness does fight you. This is a good fake, not a permanent answer.

name: Oyster sauce stand-in
blurb: Two routes, depending on whether you want the thickness or the savour.
method: For body: thin the hoisin with fish sauce and a splash of water until it pours like syrup.
For savour: Worcestershire is anchovy-based, so soy, Worcestershire and palm sugar give you the same backbone without the gloss.
note: You own the real thing now. Keep this for when the bottle runs out mid-cook.

name: Mirin stand-in
blurb: Fine in a cooked glaze, wrong in anything raw.
method: Dissolve the palm sugar in warm water.
Add the vinegar. Use immediately.
note: You have real mirin now. This is for the day you do not.

name: Seasoned rice vinegar
blurb: Better than the bottled stuff, and it takes ninety seconds.
method: Warm gently until the sugar and salt dissolve. Do not boil.
Cool before using.
note: Drop the sugar to 1 part if you want it sharp rather than balanced.

name: Chinese sesame paste from tahini
blurb: Chinese sesame paste is made from toasted seeds and tahini is not, which is why straight swaps taste flat and faintly bitter. This closes the gap.
method: Dry-toast the sesame seeds in a pan until deep brown and loudly fragrant.
Grind them to a paste in a mortar or spice grinder.
Stir into the tahini with the sesame oil. Do the whole jar at once.
note: Gets you to about 95% of the real thing instead of 80%.
keeps: As long as the tahini would have

name: Toasted rice powder
blurb: Nutty, gritty, and it thickens a dressing without adding fat. Costs nothing and it is the whole trick behind jaew and larb.
method: Dry-toast raw rice in a pan over medium heat, moving constantly, until deep brown.
Cool, then grind to a coarse powder. Leave it gritty.
keeps: A month in a jar, though it fades

name: Chili garlic oil
blurb: A rough chili crisp. Improves about half of everything else on this list.
method: Heat the oil gently with the sliced garlic until the garlic is pale gold. Do not let it go brown in the pot.
Pour the hot oil over the crushed chili and salt in a heatproof bowl.
Finish with sesame oil once it has stopped sizzling.
keeps: Weeks, and it improves for the first few days

name: Mala oil
blurb: Numbing and hot. The base under dan dan noodles, mapo tofu and every cold noodle dressing worth eating.

ingredients.sub: 1 part doenjang + 2 parts gochugaru, used lightly

method: Heat the oil with the star anise and Sichuan peppercorns until fragrant, not smoking.
Strain out the whole spices.
Pour the hot oil over the crushed chili and doubanjiang. Stir and let it settle.
note: Use the sediment, not just the clear oil. The sediment is the point.

name: Dumpling dipping sauce
blurb: The two-ingredient standard, plus ginger if you have it.
method: Stir together in a saucer. That is all of it.

name: All-purpose stir-fry sauce
blurb: The workhorse. Mix a jar and it covers weeknights indefinitely.
method: Combine everything but the cornstarch.
Add to the wok in the last thirty seconds.
If you want it to cling, add a cornstarch slurry and let it bubble once.
note: Dark soy is colour and a faint molasses depth, not salt. A quarter teaspoon is often right.

name: Red-braise base
blurb: Caramel first, then soy. The colour comes from both.
method: Melt the palm sugar in a little oil until it darkens.
Add the aromatics, then the meat, and let it colour.
Add both soys and water to cover. Simmer low and long until the liquid is glossy.

name: Kung pao sauce
blurb: Your black vinegar substitute actually shines here, because the sugar in the balsamic is already part of the balance.
method: Bloom the whole chilies and peppercorns in oil until the chilies darken.
Add garlic and ginger, then the protein.
Pour in the premixed sauce and toss until it grips.

name: Char siu glaze
blurb: Missing red fermented bean curd, but it roasts beautifully.
method: Marinate pork shoulder or belly strips overnight.
Roast hot, basting twice, until the edges char.
note: The sweetest thing on this list. Cut the palm sugar by half if that matters to you.

name: Ginger scallion sauce
blurb: Three ingredients and hot oil. Goes on poached chicken, rice, noodles, fish, everything.
method: Combine ginger, scallion, garlic and salt in a heatproof bowl.
Pour smoking oil over. It should hiss hard.
Stir in sesame oil once it settles.

name: Fish-fragrant sauce
blurb: No fish in it. Traditionally sugar-balanced, but taken down to a third the vinegar leads and it suits you better.

ingredients.sub: 1 part doenjang + 2 parts gochugaru, used sparingly

method: Fry the doubanjiang in oil until the oil turns red.
Add garlic, ginger and scallion whites for thirty seconds.
Add the premixed liquid, bubble, then finish with scallion greens.

name: Zhajiang
blurb: Salty, dark and not sweet. Cook it until the oil separates and comes back up.
method: Brown the pork hard until it is properly crisp at the edges.
Add aromatics, then the pastes, and cook down slowly.
It is ready when the oil separates and pools red at the edge.

name: Cold vegetable dressing
blurb: Smash a cucumber with the flat of a knife, salt it, drain it, and toss it in this.
method: Whisk together and let it stand ten minutes so the garlic softens.
Toss through cold vegetables just before serving.

name: Mouth-watering chicken dressing
blurb: Nominally has a little sugar in it. Leave it out and the vinegar and peppercorn carry it.
method: Poach chicken gently and cool it in its own liquid.
Tear by hand, pile on a plate, flood with the dressing.

name: Hot and sour base
blurb: In Chinese cooking the hot in hot and sour is white pepper, not chili. This is where your white peppercorns matter.

ingredients.amount: 1.5 tsp, freshly ground, more than feels right

method: Build a stock with mushrooms and tofu if making soup, then season with this at the end.
Vinegar and pepper both fade with heat. Add half at the start and half off the heat.

name: Dan dan sauce
blurb: Loosen with hot noodle water, not more oil. Barely any sugar belongs in it.
method: Whisk the sesame paste with the soy first, adding hot water a spoon at a time until smooth.
Stir in everything else.
Pool it in the bottom of the bowl and drop hot noodles on top. Toss at the table.
note: Without ya cai you have sesame noodles, which is a different and lesser dish.

name: Bang bang chicken dressing
blurb: The cold version of dan dan, and sharper: more vinegar, more chili oil, thinner.
method: Lay cucumber down first, chicken on top, dressing over.
Do not slice the chicken. Tearing gives the sauce something to hold.

name: Sesame paste cold noodles
blurb: Summer food. Make it in the morning, eat it cold at two in the afternoon.
method: Thin the paste with cold water until it ribbons off the spoon.
Toss with cold noodles and shredded cucumber.

name: Sichuan cold noodle dressing
blurb: Sour, citrusy and tingling. Squarely built for a palate that wants sour and hot and nothing sweet.
method: Toast the green peppercorns until they smell like lime peel, then crush.
Whisk everything and let it sit fifteen minutes before using.
note: Green Sichuan peppercorn is far more citrusy than the red. Use it where you would want lime zest.

name: Tonkatsu and okonomiyaki sauce
blurb: The best trick in the pantry. A1 is structurally close to Bulldog sauce: tomato, vinegar, fruit puree.
method: Stir together cold.
For okonomiyaki, push it sweeter with more hoisin. For katsu, leave it sharp.

name: Yakisoba sauce
blurb: Worcestershire-led, because that is genuinely what it is.
method: Mix, then toss with the noodles in the last twenty seconds so it catches on the pan.

name: Teriyaki glaze
blurb: Now that you have real mirin, the honest ratio works.
method: Simmer until it coats the back of a spoon.
Brush on in the last minutes of cooking, not before, or it burns.

name: Goma dare
blurb: This one wants restraint, not chili.
method: Whisk the paste with the liquids gradually until it pours smoothly.

name: Nanbanzuke
blurb: Japanese escabeche. Fry it hot, drown it, eat it cold the next day.

ingredients.amount: 2 tbsp, halved for a sharper version

method: Fry the fish or chicken until crisp.
Drop it straight into the warm marinade with the vegetables.
Refrigerate overnight. It is better on day two.
note: Red wine vinegar works better than balsamic here if you want it drier.

name: Yuzu kosho, approximated
blurb: Not the real thing without yuzu zest, but it hits the same citrus-salt-heat note and goes on everything.
method: Mince the chilies with the salt until they break down.
Mash to a paste with the ponzu.
Jar it and leave three days before using.

name: Ponzu with chili and ginger
blurb: Two minutes, and your ponzu is doing a lot of unglamorous work.
method: Combine. Serve within the hour while the ginger is still sharp.

name: Sesame ginger dressing
blurb: The one to make when you want a salad to taste like something.
method: Shake in a jar. It splits, so shake again before pouring.

name: Ssamjang
blurb: The real recipe, now that the doenjang is confirmed. This is what makes it taste Korean rather than Chinese.
method: Mash together. Add the onion if you want texture rather than a smooth paste.

name: Bulgogi marinade
blurb: Grated apple or pear tenderises and rounds it out, if you can get one.
method: Marinate thin-sliced beef two hours or overnight.
Cook fast over high heat so the sugar caramelises rather than stews.

name: Yangnyeomjang
blurb: The Korean equivalent of sawsawan. Make it weekly and put it on everything.
method: Stir together and leave twenty minutes for the gochugaru to swell and go red.

name: Oi muchim
blurb: Sour, hot, cold, and not sweet. Squarely your palate.
method: Salt the cucumber, wait twenty minutes, squeeze out the water.
Toss with everything else. Eat within the hour.

name: Geotjeori
blurb: Fresh unfermented kimchi. All the flavour, none of the waiting.
method: Salt the cut cabbage for an hour, then rinse and drain hard.
Toss with everything else using your hands.
Eat the same day.
uses: In fried rice the next day

name: Bibim sauce, sugar cut
blurb: The standard recipe is sugar-heavy. Drop it entirely, let vinegar carry, and it turns into a sour-spicy dressing.
method: Whisk. Thin with a spoon of water if it is too stiff to toss.

name: Red stew base
blurb: Blooming the gochugaru in oil is what makes it taste red instead of dusty.
method: Bloom the gochugaru in sesame oil with the garlic over low heat until the oil goes red.
Stir in the pastes, then add stock.
Simmer, add tofu and whatever vegetable is around.

name: Doenjang jjigae
blurb: Salty and deeply funky with zero sweetness. Squarely your thing.

ingredients.sub: anchovy stock is correct, plain works

method: Whisk the doenjang into the stock so it dissolves before it boils.
Simmer fifteen minutes with the garlic, then add tofu and vegetables.
Finish with scallion off the heat.

name: Namul seasoning
blurb: The quiet unlock. Five minutes, and it is the reason Korean side dishes taste the way they do.
method: Blanch the vegetable briefly, shock it cold, squeeze out every drop of water.
Toss with the seasoning using your hands.

name: Doenjang vinaigrette
blurb: Cuts through grilled meat and roasted vegetables better than anything else in the pantry.
method: Whisk the doenjang with the vinegar first, then the oil, then water to the thickness you want.

name: Doenjang marinade
blurb: Grill or roast hard so the paste chars. The char is the reason to make it.
method: Coat and marinate at least four hours.
Wipe off the excess before it hits the heat, or it burns before the meat cooks.

name: Doenjang butter
blurb: Not Korean, not traditional, and worth making anyway. Miso butter's angrier cousin.
method: Mash together, roll in paper, refrigerate. Slice off coins as needed.

name: Gochujang tahini dressing
blurb: Not traditional anywhere. The tahini kills gochujang's sweetness, which is exactly what you want it to do.
method: Whisk, adding water last until it drizzles.

name: Vietnamese caramel
blurb: Two ingredients, enormous payoff. Take the caramel darker than feels comfortable.

ingredients.amount: roughly equal to the finished caramel

method: Melt the palm sugar dry over medium heat until it goes dark amber and just starts to smell bitter.
Kill the heat with water, standing back.
Add fish sauce roughly one to one with the caramel.
note: The bitterness at the edge of the caramel is what keeps the dish from being sweet.

name: Nuoc cham
blurb: Adjust until it tastes like something you could drink.

ingredients.sub: yuzu ponzu for the citrus note

method: Dissolve the sugar in warm water first.
Add everything else and taste. It should be balanced, not sharp.
note: Cut the sugar by half and push the citrus if you want it sour-forward.

name: Green chili salt
blurb: Violent, citrusy, addictive. The best thing that has ever happened to grilled squid.
method: Blitz everything to a rough green paste. Do not make it smooth.

name: Nam jim
blurb: Sharper and more aromatic than nuoc cham, and it wants to be made fresh.
method: Pound the garlic and chili in a mortar, or mince very fine.
Stir in the liquids. Taste for sour first, then salt, then sweet.

name: Jaew
blurb: Probably the best fit on this entire list for a palate that wants sour, citrus and heat with no sugar.
method: Toast raw rice in a dry pan until deep brown, then grind coarse.
Combine everything and let it sit ten minutes so the rice powder swells.
It should be thick enough to cling to grilled meat.
note: The toasted rice powder is the whole trick. Nutty, gritty, and it thickens without fat.

name: Prik nam pla
nativeName: พริกน้ำปลา
blurb: Sits on every table in Thailand. Make it and put it on eggs.
method: Combine in a small bowl. It is ready immediately and better after an hour.
uses: Any Thai dish that needs sharpening

name: Sinamak
blurb: Ilonggo spiced vinegar, and your peppercorn collection is made for it. It gets sharper and better for months.

ingredients.sub: cane vinegar is correct; rice vinegar also works

method: Pack everything into a jar and cover with vinegar.
Leave two weeks before touching it.
Top up with vinegar as you use it.

name: Toyomansi
blurb: Two minutes, and it is the default dip for grilled meat and fried fish.
method: Stir together in a saucer.
note: Calamansi is floral-sour with a bitter edge, which is why ponzu slots in so cleanly.

name: Suka't bawang
blurb: Deliberately harsh. That is the point.
method: Combine and let it stand an hour so the garlic mellows slightly.
A pinch of MSG and a few drops of fish sauce fake the funk that cane vinegar has and cider does not.

name: Patis at calamansi
blurb: A salt-and-acid slap for anything that needs waking up.
method: Combine. Serve in a shallow saucer so you can dip rather than pour.

name: Sawsawan for inihaw
blurb: Slightly sweeter than the rest, and meant for grilled pork.
method: Stir together and let it sit while the grill heats.

name: Lechon sauce, improvised
blurb: Where your A1 earns its keep a second time. The real thing is liver-based, so it will not be identical, but the sweet-sour-savoury shape is right.
method: Warm everything gently until the breadcrumbs swell and it thickens.
Thin with water if it sets too far.

name: Adobo
blurb: You can make this tonight. Not sweet at all in its honest form.
method: Combine everything cold in the pot and bring to a simmer.
Do not stir for the first ten minutes. Let the vinegar cook off its raw edge.
Simmer until tender, then reduce hard so it glazes.

name: Schezwan chutney
blurb: The Indian one, unrelated to actual Sichuan cooking. Goes on noodles, rice, eggs and sandwiches.
method: Soak the dried chilies until soft, then blend with garlic, ginger, vinegar and salt.
Fry the paste in oil over medium heat until it darkens and the oil separates out.
Cool completely before jarring.
note: Skip any fermented bean paste here. Chilies, garlic, ginger and vinegar carry it on their own.
keeps: A month, refrigerated under a film of oil

name: Manchurian sauce
blurb: Restaurant versions are cloying. Skip the sugar entirely and it is sharp and savoury.
method: Fry garlic, ginger, chili and scallion whites hard in hot oil.
Add the liquids and chili paste, bring to a boil.
Thicken with cornstarch slurry, then toss with fried vegetable balls or chicken.

name: Indo-Chinese chili garlic noodles
blurb: The tell is a quarter teaspoon of garam masala hitting the wok at the end. Sounds wrong, tastes right.
method: Get the wok hot enough to hurt. Fry the garlic and chili for fifteen seconds.
Add noodles and the liquids, toss hard.
Off the heat, dust with garam masala and scatter scallion.
note: Worcestershire is the historical link here. It descends from a tamarind and anchovy Anglo-Indian sauce.

name: Pad thai sauce
blurb: Restaurant versions are dessert. Tamarind and fish sauce carry it; hold the sugar down and it tastes like food again.
method: Soak block tamarind in hot water, work it with a fork, and push it through a sieve.
Warm everything until the palm sugar dissolves. Taste: sour first, salt behind it, sweet last.
About three tablespoons per portion of noodles, into a hot pan.
note: The classic ratio is equal parts. Starting the sugar at two-thirds is deliberate.

name: Sinigang base
blurb: The souring packets are mostly salt and citric acid. Real tamarind gives the broth some body behind its pucker.
method: Simmer the tamarind pulp in a cup of the stock, mash it, and strain back into the pot.
Simmer the meat with onion and tomato until tender, then add vegetables in order of toughness.
Season with fish sauce off the heat. It should make you wince a little.
note: Sourness fades as it sits. Err past where you want it.

name: Nam prik pao
nativeName: น้ำพริกเผา
blurb: Thai chili jam, and what makes tom yum taste like a restaurant's. Sweeter than it looks. Treat the sugar as a ceiling.
method: Fry shallots, then garlic, then chilies in the oil, each until just past golden. Do not walk away.
Blend the fried things with the dried shrimp, loosened with the frying oil.
Cook the paste back down with tamarind, palm sugar and fish sauce until it darkens to jam.
keeps: A month, refrigerated under a film of oil

name: Tamarind fish sauce
blurb: Nuoc cham's darker cousin. Tamarind instead of lime, cooked until it just coats a spoon. Made for fried fish.
method: Simmer tamarind, water and palm sugar until slightly thickened.
Off the heat, add fish sauce, garlic and chili.
Serve warm. It tightens as it cools.
note: Sweeter than nuoc cham by design, but two tablespoons is already generous. Taste before adding more.

name: Imli chutney
blurb: The sweet-sour one on every chaat. It is honestly sweet, because that is the job. Make it rarely and make it count.
method: Simmer everything until it coats a spoon, about fifteen minutes.
Push through a sieve and cool. It thickens further as it sets.
note: Cutting the sugar here breaks it. If sweetness 3 is off the table tonight, reach for the schezwan chutney instead.

name: Spicy mayo
blurb: Two things stirred together and still the most requested sauce in any house. The sriracha is already sweet; it needs nothing else.

ingredients.amount: a pinch, when it needs to bite harder

method: Stir and taste. The ratio is a preference, not a formula.
Let it sit ten minutes so the garlic in the sriracha blooms.

name: Ginataan base
blurb: Coconut milk cooked past creamy into sauce. The Bicol formula: coconut, chili and shrimp paste, no compromise on any of the three.

ingredients.amount: 2 cans; one to simmer, one to finish

ingredients.sub: 3 tbsp fish sauce, quieter but it works

ingredients.amount: 4-6, and that is the mild version
belly, or shrimp, or squash and greens

method: Simmer the first can until the oil splits out, then fry the aromatics in that oil.
Add the meat and bagoong, then the second can. Keep it under a boil.
Reduce until it clings. Watery gata is the common failure.
note: The sweetness rating is the coconut itself. Do not add sugar.

name: Tom kha base
blurb: Galangal, lemongrass and makrut leaves are the real spine. This is the version your pantry can field tonight, and it still earns the pot.

ingredients.amount: 6 thick slices, standing in for galangal
2 tbsp off the heat, doing lime duty

method: Simmer the ginger and chili in the stock for ten minutes.
Add coconut milk and chicken and keep it under a boil. Coconut milk splits at a gallop.
Off the heat, fish sauce and ponzu. Cooked citrus goes dull.
